name: Antimilitarism
summary: Antimilitarism opposes militarism: a society in which war or preparation for war dominates politics, and the political power of a large standing army. It is not pacifism: the defining sources accept citizen militias and some wars, and the socialist tradition (Liebknecht's Militarism and Anti-Militarism, the Second International's congress resolutions) ties militarism to capitalism and class rule.
scope: The reference definition (the Oxford Companion entry) and the socialist antimilitarism of the Second International as set out in Karl Liebknecht's 1907 Militarism and Anti-Militarism (congress resolutions 1868-1900, the German minimum programme). The American tradition against standing armies and Eisenhower's farewell warning are named by the Oxford Companion but state no further positions here. Excluded: absolute pacifism, and the platforms of peace organisations or the positions of states such as Japan (Article 9), which are coatracks.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Liebknecht's account of the Social-Democratic programme repudiates the stance directed against every kind of preparation for war and asks for a citizen army and reduced arms, not abolition; the Oxford Companion says antimilitarism is not pacifist resistance to all war.

missingStatements.text: Military spending should be cut and the money spent on health, education and development.
missingStatements.rationale: Eisenhower called weapons a theft from the hungry, and the article names diversion of resources from development as a core objection.

missingStatements.text: Standing armies are dangerous to a free people and should be replaced by citizen militias.
missingStatements.rationale: Paris 1899 called standing armies the negation of democratic republics and demanded a citizen army, and Jefferson-style constitutionalists agree.

missingStatements.text: Private arms manufacturers have too much influence over defence and foreign policy.
missingStatements.rationale: Eisenhower warned against the military-industrial complex and the article reports the charge that it pushes for war for private gain.

missingStatements.text: Armed forces should be used only to defend the country against attack, never to start wars.
missingStatements.rationale: Antimilitarism accepts defensive war but opposes aggressive readiness, and Article 9 renounces war as a means of settling disputes.

missingStatements.text: The people should decide whether their country goes to war.
missingStatements.rationale: Both the London 1896 resolution and the German minimum programme Liebknecht sets out demand that the people decide on war and peace.

notes: Later pass (2026-11-13) answering from the defining sources: the Oxford Companion entry on militarism and antimilitarism and Liebknecht's 1907 book with the Second International resolutions it reviews. The earlier answers rested on Wikipedia's tour of strands (Thoreau, Japan's Article 9, right-wing militia movements) and general outlook; they are nulled unless a defining source settles them. Themes searched: definitions of the term, standing armies and citizen militias, conscription, disarmament and arms reduction, war and capitalism, alliances, colonial militarism, military budgets, youth education, soldiers' refusal, Eisenhower's farewell address (which also says arms must be mighty, so it does not settle arms or spending statements). Economy, society, culture, ecology and liberty themes remain unanswered because the sources say nothing on them; an uncertainty-rule failure is the honest result.
